On March 12, 2014, a Florida jury found in favor of Gotta Have It on its breach of contract and other related claims, rejected ETW's counterclaims, and awarded Gotta Have It $668,346 in damages.[[176]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-178) The award may end up exceeding $1 million once interest has been factored in, though the ruling may be appealed.

In August 2016, Woods announced that he would be seeking a new golf equipment partner[[177]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-179) after the news of Nike's exit from the equipment industry.[[178]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-180) It was announced on January 25, 2017, that he would be signing a new club deal with [TaylorMade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TaylorMade-Adidas "TaylorMade-Adidas").[[179]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-181) He added the 2016 M2 driver along with the 2017 M1 fairway woods, with irons to be custom made at a later date. He also added his [Scotty Cameron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scotty_Cameron "Scotty Cameron") Newport 2 GSS, a club he used to win 13 of his 15 majors.[[180]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-182) Also, in late 2016, he would add [Monster Energy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monster_Energy "Monster Energy") as his primary bag sponsor, replacing MusclePharm.[[181]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-183)

On January 8, 2024, Woods announced that he would be parting ways with Nike after 27 years, ending one of the most lucrative endorsements any athlete has had.[[182]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-184)

### Accumulated wealth

Woods has appeared on [Forbes list of the world's highest-paid athletes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forbes_list_of_the_world's_highest-paid_athletes "Forbes list of the world's highest-paid athletes").[[183]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-decree-185)[[184]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-186) According to _Golf Digest_, Woods earned $769,440,709 from 1996 to 2007,[[185]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-187) and the magazine predicted that Woods would pass a billion dollars in earnings by 2010.[[186]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-188) In 2009, _[Forbes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forbes "Forbes")_ confirmed that Woods was indeed the world's first professional athlete to earn over a billion dollars in his career, after accounting for the $10 million bonus Woods received for the [FedEx Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FedEx_Cup "FedEx Cup") title.[[187]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-189) The same year, Forbes estimated his net worth to be $600 million, making him the second [richest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_billionaires "Black billionaires")[person of color](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Person_of_color "Person of color") in the U.S., behind only [Oprah Winfrey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oprah_Winfrey "Oprah Winfrey").[[188]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-190) In 2015, Woods ranked ninth in [Forbes list of the world's highest-paid athletes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forbes_list_of_the_world's_highest-paid_athletes "Forbes list of the world's highest-paid athletes"), being the top among Asian Americans or the fourth among African Americans.[[189]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-191) As of 2017, Woods was considered to be the highest-paid golfer in the world.[[190]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-192) In 2022, Woods was the first golfer to have a net worth over one billion dollars,[[191]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-193) making him one of the [richest celebrities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_celebrities_by_net_worth "List of celebrities by net worth").

### Tiger-proofing

Early in Woods's career, a small number of golf industry analysts expressed concern about his impact on the competitiveness of the game and the public appeal of professional golf. Sportswriter Bill Lyon of [Knight Ridder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Knight_Ridder "Knight Ridder") asked in a column, "Isn't Tiger Woods actually bad for golf?" (though Lyon ultimately concluded that he was not).[[192]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-Bad-194) At first, some pundits feared that Woods would drive the spirit of competition out of the game of golf by making existing courses obsolete and relegating opponents to simply competing for second place each week.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

A related effect was measured by [University of California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_California,_Berkeley "University of California, Berkeley") economist Jennifer Brown, who found that other golfers scored worse when competing against Woods than when he was not in the tournament. The scores of highly skilled golfers are nearly one stroke higher when playing against Woods. This effect was larger when he was on winning streaks and disappeared during his well-publicized slump in 2003–04. Brown explains the results by noting that competitors of similar skill can hope to win by increasing their level of effort, but that, when facing a "superstar" competitor, extra exertion does not significantly raise one's level of winning while increasing risk of injury or exhaustion, leading to reduced effort.[[193]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-195) Many courses in the PGA Tour rotation (including major championship sites like [Augusta National](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augusta_National_Golf_Club "Augusta National Golf Club")) have added yardage to their tees in an effort to reduce the advantage of long hitters like Woods, in a strategy that became known as "Tiger-proofing".[[194]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-196) Woods said he welcomed the change, in that adding yardage to courses did not affect his ability to win.[[195]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-Open2005-197)

## Career achievements

Main article: [List of career achievements by Tiger Woods](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_career_achievements_by_Tiger_Woods "List of career achievements by Tiger Woods")

Woods has won 82 official [PGA Tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PGA_Tour "PGA Tour") events, including 15 [majors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Men's_major_golf_championships "Men's major golf championships"). He is 14–1 when going into the final round of a major with at least a share of the lead. Multiple golf experts have heralded Woods as "the greatest closer in history".[[196]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-198) He has the lowest career scoring average and the largest career earnings of any player in PGA Tour history.

Woods's victory at the [2013 Players Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2013_Players_Championship "2013 Players Championship") also marked a win in his 300th [PGA Tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PGA_Tour "PGA Tour") start.[[197]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-199) He also won golf tournaments in his [100th](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WGC-Bridgestone_Invitational#Winners "WGC-Bridgestone Invitational") (in 2000) and [200th](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Farmers_Insurance_Open#Winners "Farmers Insurance Open") (in 2006) tour starts.[[198]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-200)

Woods has spent the most consecutive and cumulative weeks atop the world rankings. He is one of six players (along with [Gene Sarazen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gene_Sarazen "Gene Sarazen"), [Ben Hogan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Hogan "Ben Hogan"), [Gary Player](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gary_Player "Gary Player"), [Jack Nicklaus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Nicklaus "Jack Nicklaus"), and [Rory McIlroy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rory_McIlroy "Rory McIlroy")) to have won all four major championships in his career, known as the Career Grand Slam, and was the youngest to do so.[[199]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-201) Woods is the only player to have consecutively won all four major championships open to professionals, accomplishing the feat in the 2000–2001 seasons.

**Eldrick Tont** "**Tiger**" **Woods** (born December 30, 1975) is an American [professional golfer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Professional_golfer "Professional golfer"). He is widely regarded as one of the greatest golfers of all time and as one of the most famous athletes in modern history.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-great-6) Woods is tied for first in [PGA Tour wins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_golfers_with_most_PGA_Tour_wins "List of golfers with most PGA Tour wins"), ranks second in [men's major championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_men's_major_championships_winning_golfers "List of men's major championships winning golfers"), holds [numerous golf records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_career_achievements_by_Tiger_Woods "List of career achievements by Tiger Woods"),[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-great-6) and is an inductee of the [World Golf Hall of Fame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Golf_Hall_of_Fame "World Golf Hall of Fame").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-7)

Following an outstanding junior, college, and amateur career, Woods turned professional in 1996 at age 20. In April 1997 he won his first major, the [1997 Masters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1997_Masters_Tournament "1997 Masters Tournament"), which he won by 12 strokes in a record-setting performance. He reached [number one](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_world_number_one_male_golfers "List of world number one male golfers") in the [Official World Golf Ranking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Official_World_Golf_Ranking "Official World Golf Ranking") for the first time in June 1997, less than a year after turning professional. At the [2000 U.S. Open](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_U.S._Open_(golf) "2000 U.S. Open (golf)") Woods won by a major record 15 strokes which is regarded by many as the greatest performance in golf history. After winning the [2001 Masters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2001_Masters_Tournament "2001 Masters Tournament") he became the only player to win four consecutive major championships in a one-year period in a feat known as the "Tiger Slam". Woods dominated men's golf throughout the first decade of the [21st century](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/21st_century "21st century"), holding the world's top ranking from August 1999 to September 2004 (264 consecutive weeks) and again from June 2005 to October 2010 (281 consecutive weeks). The following decade was marked by comebacks from personal issues and injuries. He took a self‑imposed hiatus from professional golf from December 2009 to April 2010 to address marital problems.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-legend-8) Woods fell to number 58 in the world rankings in November 2011 before returning to the number‑one position between March 2013 and May 2014.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-Westwood-9)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-chevron-10) Injuries led to four [back surgeries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discectomy "Discectomy") between 2014 and 2017,[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-11) and he competed in only one tournament between August 2015 and January 2018, dropping out of the world's top 1,000 players.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-12)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-reid-13) After returning to regular competition, he won the [Tour Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tour_Championship "Tour Championship") in September 2018—his first victory in five years—and the [2019 Masters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_Masters_Tournament "2019 Masters Tournament"), his first major in 11 years.

Woods holds numerous golf records. He has spent the most consecutive weeks and the most total weeks as the world's number‑one player. He has been named [PGA Player of the Year](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PGA_Player_of_the_Year "PGA Player of the Year") a record 11 times,[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-14) and he led the PGA Tour [money list](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PGA_Tour#Money_winners_and_most_wins_leaders "PGA Tour") in 10 seasons. He has won 15 [major golf championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Men's_major_golf_championships "Men's major golf championships") (second only to [Jack Nicklaus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Nicklaus "Jack Nicklaus")'s 18) and 82 PGA Tour events (tied with [Sam Snead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam_Snead "Sam Snead") for the all-time record).[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-15) Woods is one of six men to complete the career [Grand Slam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Slam_(golf) "Grand Slam (golf)"), along with [Gene Sarazen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gene_Sarazen "Gene Sarazen"), [Ben Hogan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Hogan "Ben Hogan"), [Gary Player](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gary_Player "Gary Player"), Nicklaus, and [Rory McIlroy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rory_McIlroy "Rory McIlroy"). He is the youngest to do so, and one of two golfers—along with Nicklaus—to achieve the career Grand Slam three times.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-16) He was a member of the winning United States team at the [1999 Ryder Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_Ryder_Cup "1999 Ryder Cup") and received the [Presidential Medal of Freedom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidential_Medal_of_Freedom "Presidential Medal of Freedom") in May 2019.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-17)

Woods was awarded [AP Athlete of the Year](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Associated_Press_Athlete_of_the_Year "Associated Press Athlete of the Year") four times and [AP Athlete of the Decade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Associated_Press "Associated Press") of the 2000s. He was also awarded _[Sports Illustrated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports\_Illustrated "Sports Illustrated")_[Sportsperson of the Year](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated_Sportsperson_of_the_Year "Sports Illustrated Sportsperson of the Year") three times and the [Laureus World Sports Sportsman of the Year](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laureus_World_Sports_Award_for_Sportsman_of_the_Year "Laureus World Sports Award for Sportsman of the Year") twice. Woods was among _[Time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time\_(magazine) "Time (magazine)")_'s [100 most influential people in the world](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_100 "Time 100") in 2004, 2009 and 2019, which is tied for the second most selections for a professional athlete. He has been listed by _[Forbes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forbes "Forbes")_ as the highest paid athlete in the world for a record 11 years, including for 10 straight years from 2002 to 2011.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-18)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-19)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-20) As of April 2026, his net worth was estimated at US$1.5 billion by _Forbes_.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-21)

On February 23, 2021, Woods was hospitalized after a single‑car collision and underwent emergency surgery for compound fractures in his right leg and a shattered ankle.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-22) In a November 2021 interview with _[Golf Digest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golf\_Digest "Golf Digest"),_ he stated that his full‑time professional career was over, though he intended to play a limited schedule.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-23) He returned to the PGA Tour at the [2022 Masters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Masters_Tournament "2022 Masters Tournament"). In 2026, Woods was involved in another car crash and reached a plea deal for willful [reckless driving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reckless_driving "Reckless driving").[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-wapo-plea-2026-24)

## Background and family

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b4/Tiger_and_Earl_Woods_Fort_Bragg_2004.jpg/250px-Tiger_and_Earl_Woods_Fort_Bragg_2004.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Tiger_and_Earl_Woods_Fort_Bragg_2004.jpg)

Woods and his father [Earl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earl_Woods "Earl Woods") at [Fort Bragg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Bragg "Fort Bragg"), [North Carolina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Carolina "North Carolina"), in 2004

Woods was born on December 30, 1975, in [Cypress, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cypress,_California "Cypress, California"), a suburb of [Los Angeles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles "Los Angeles").[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-25) He is the only child of [Earl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earl_Woods "Earl Woods")[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-26) and Kultida "Tida" Woods ([née](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birth_name#Maiden_and_married_names "Birth name")Punsawad).[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-27) He has two half‑brothers and a half‑sister from his father's first marriage.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-28) Earl, a retired U.S. Army officer and [Vietnam War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vietnam_War "Vietnam War") veteran, was born to African-American parents and was also described as having European, Chinese, and [Native American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Native_Americans_in_the_United_States "Native Americans in the United States") ([Cherokee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cherokee "Cherokee")) ancestry.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-earlna-29)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-30)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-31) Kultida was originally from [Thailand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thailand "Thailand"), where she met Earl during his tour of duty in 1968. She was of mixed Thai, Chinese, and Dutch descent.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-Stripes-32) In 2002, ESPN stated that Woods was "one-quarter Thai, one-quarter Chinese, one-quarter Caucasian, one-eighth African American and one-eighth Native American."[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-ESPN_stripes-33) Woods has described his ethnic background as "Cablinasian", a term he coined from Caucasian, Black, American Indian, and Asian.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-Cablinasian-34)

His mother chose his first name, Eldrick, because it began with "E" (for Earl) and ended with "K" (for Kultida). His middle name, Tont, is a traditional Thai name. He was nicknamed Tiger in honor of his father's friend, [South Vietnamese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Vietnam "South Vietnam") colonel Vuong Dang Phong, who was also known as "Tiger".[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-35) Woods's niece, [Cheyenne Woods](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cheyenne_Woods "Cheyenne Woods"), played collegiate golf at [Wake Forest University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wake_Forest_Demon_Deacons "Wake Forest Demon Deacons") and turned professional in 2012, making her debut at the [LPGA Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LPGA_Championship "LPGA Championship").[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-36)

Earl died on May 3, 2006. Kultida died on February 4, 2025. Following his mother's death, Woods stated that "without her none of my personal achievements would have been possible."[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-37)

## Early life and amateur golf career

Eldrick Tont Woods was born on December 30, 1975, in Cypress, California, a suburb of Los Angeles. A child prodigy, he was introduced to golf before the age of two by his father, an accomplished athlete who was a single‑digit‑handicap amateur golfer and one of the earliest African American college [baseball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baseball "Baseball") players at [Kansas State University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_State_University "Kansas State University").[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-38) Woods later said he had once hoped to become a baseball player like his father but abandoned that goal after [tearing his rotator cuff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rotator_cuff_tear "Rotator cuff tear").[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-39) Because his father was a member of the military, he had playing privileges at the Navy Golf Course adjacent to the [Joint Forces Training Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joint_Forces_Training_Base_-_Los_Alamitos "Joint Forces Training Base - Los Alamitos") in [Los Alamitos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Alamitos,_California "Los Alamitos, California"), which allowed Woods to play there. Woods also played at the par-3 Heartwell Golf Course in [Long Beach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long_Beach,_California "Long Beach, California") and at several Long beach [municipal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golf_course#Municipal "Golf course") courses.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-40)

In 1978, Woods putted against comedian [Bob Hope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Hope "Bob Hope") during a television appearance on _[The Mike Douglas Show](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Mike\_Douglas\_Show "The Mike Douglas Show")_. At age three, he shot a 48 over nine holes at the Navy course. At age five, he appeared in _[Golf Digest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golf\_Digest "Golf Digest")_ and on [ABC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Broadcasting_Company "American Broadcasting Company")'s _[That's Incredible!](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/That's\_Incredible! "That's Incredible!")._[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-Timeline-41) Before turning seven, Woods won the Under‑Age‑10 division of the Drive, Pitch, and Putt competition at the Navy Golf Course in Cypress.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-42) In 1984, at age eight, he won the 9–10 boys' event—the youngest available age group—at the [Junior World Golf Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Junior_World_Golf_Championships "Junior World Golf Championships").[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-JWGC84-43) He first broke 80 at age eight.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-44) Woods went on to win the Junior World Championships six times, including four consecutive titles from 1988 to 1991.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-JWGC85-45)[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-JWGC88-46)[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-JWGC89-47)[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-JWGC90-48)[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-JWGC91-49) His father later wrote that Woods first defeated him at age 11, with Earl playing his best; Earl never beat Woods again.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-50) Woods first broke 70 on a regulation course at age 12.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-callahan1-51)

At age 13, Woods played in the 1989 Big I, his first major national junior tournament. In the final round, he was paired with professional golfer [John Daly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Daly_(golfer) "John Daly (golfer)"), then relatively unknown. The event's format placed one professional with each group of juniors. Daly birdied three of the last four holes to defeat Woods by a single stroke.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-52) As a young teenager, Woods met [Jack Nicklaus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Nicklaus "Jack Nicklaus") at the [Bel-Air Country Club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel-Air_Country_Club "Bel-Air Country Club") in Los Angeles, where Nicklaus was conducting a clinic. Woods participated in the exhibition and impressed Nicklaus and the audience with his skill and potential.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-53) His father had extensively studied Nicklaus's records and set those achievements as goals for his son.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-callahan1-51)

At age 15, while attending [Western High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_High_School_(Anaheim,_California) "Western High School (Anaheim, California)") in Anaheim, Woods became the youngest [U.S. Junior Amateur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Junior_Amateur "U.S. Junior Amateur") champion, a record that stood until Jim Liu broke it in 2010.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-USJA91-54) Woods was named the 1991 Southern California Amateur Player of the Year (for the second consecutive year) and the Golf Digest Junior Amateur Player of the Year. In 1992, Woods successfully defended his U.S. Junior Amateur title, becoming the event's first two‑time winner. That year he also competed in his first PGA Tour event, the [Nissan Los Angeles Open](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nissan_Los_Angeles_Open "Nissan Los Angeles Open") (he missed the 36-hole cut), and was named _Golf Digest_ Amateur Player of the Year, _[Golf World](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golf\_World "Golf World")_ Player of the Year, and _[Golfweek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golfweek "Golfweek")_ National Amateur of the Year.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-USJA92-55)[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-IMG-56)

Woods won his third consecutive U.S. Junior Amateur the following year, remaining the event's only three‑time champion.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-USJA93-57) In 1994, at [TPC Sawgrass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TPC_at_Sawgrass "TPC at Sawgrass") in Florida, he became the youngest winner of the [U.S. Amateur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Amateur "U.S. Amateur"), a record that stood until 2008 when it was broken by [Danny Lee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danny_Lee_(golfer) "Danny Lee (golfer)").[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-Sounes,_p._277-58)[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-59) He represented the U.S. at the 1994 [Eisenhower Trophy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eisenhower_Trophy "Eisenhower Trophy")[World Amateur Golf Team Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Amateur_Golf_Team_Championships "World Amateur Golf Team Championships") (winning) and the 1995 [Walker Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walker_Cup "Walker Cup") (losing).[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-IGF-60)[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-Walker-61)

Woods graduated from Western High School in 1994 at age 18 and was voted "Most Likely to Succeed" by his classmates. He starred on the school's golf team under coach Don Crosby.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-62) As a child, Woods learned to manage a [stutter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stuttering "Stuttering").[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-63) This became publicly known when he wrote a letter to a boy who had contemplated suicide, telling him: "I know what it's like to be different and to sometimes not fit in. I also stuttered as a child and I would talk to my dog and he would sit there and listen until he fell asleep. I also took a class for two years to help me, and I finally learned to stop."[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-64)

## College golf career

Woods was heavily recruited by college golf powers and chose [Stanford University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_Cardinal "Stanford Cardinal"), the reigning [NCAA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Collegiate_Athletic_Association "National Collegiate Athletic Association")[champions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NCAA_Division_I_men's_golf_championship "NCAA Division I men's golf championship").[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-wbputr-65) He enrolled at Stanford in the fall of 1994 under a golf [scholarship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletic_scholarship "Athletic scholarship") and won his first collegiate event, the 40th Annual William H. Tucker Invitational, that September.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-Stanford-66) He selected a major in economics and was nicknamed "[Urkel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Urkel "Steve Urkel")" by college teammate [Notah Begay III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Notah_Begay_III "Notah Begay III").[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-67) In 1995, he successfully defended his U.S. Amateur title at the [Newport Country Club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newport_Country_Club "Newport Country Club") in [Rhode Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhode_Island "Rhode Island")[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-Sounes,_p._277-58) and was voted Pac-10 Player of the Year, NCAA First Team All-American, and Stanford's Male Freshman of the Year (an award that encompasses all sports).[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-PAC10-68)[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-Ages-69)

At age 19, Woods participated in his first PGA Tour major, the [1995 Masters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1995_Masters_Tournament "1995 Masters Tournament"), and tied for 41st as the only amateur to make the cut. At age 20 in 1996, he became the first golfer to win three consecutive U.S. Amateur titles[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-70) and won the [NCAA individual golf championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NCAA_Division_I_Men's_Golf_Championships "NCAA Division I Men's Golf Championships").[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-NCAA-71) In winning the silver medal as leading amateur at [The Open Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1996_Open_Championship "1996 Open Championship"), he tied the record for an amateur aggregate score of 281.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-Open1996-72) He left college after two years in order to turn professional in the golf industry. In 1996, Woods moved out of California, stating in 2013 that it was due to the state's high tax rate.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-73)

## Professional career

Main article: [Professional golf career of Tiger Woods](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Professional_golf_career_of_Tiger_Woods "Professional golf career of Tiger Woods")

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/ea/TigerWoods1997.jpg/250px-TigerWoods1997.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:TigerWoods1997.jpg)

Woods in 1997

Woods turned [professional](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Professional_golfer "Professional golfer") at age 20 in August 1996 and immediately signed [advertising deals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Testimonial "Testimonial") with [Nike, Inc.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nike,_Inc. "Nike, Inc.") and [Titleist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Titleist "Titleist") that ranked as the most lucrative endorsement [contracts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contract "Contract") in golf history at that time.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-10Years1-74)[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-Hello-75) Woods was named _[Sports Illustrated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports\_Illustrated "Sports Illustrated")_'s 1996 [Sportsman of the Year](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated_Sportsperson_of_the_Year "Sports Illustrated Sportsperson of the Year") and [PGA Tour Rookie of the Year](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PGA_Tour_Rookie_of_the_Year "PGA Tour Rookie of the Year").[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-SI1996-76) On April 13, 1997, he won his first [major](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Men's_major_golf_championships "Men's major golf championships"), [the Masters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1997_Masters_Tournament "1997 Masters Tournament"), in record-breaking fashion and became the tournament's youngest winner at age 21.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-10Years2-77) Two months later, he set the record for the fastest ascent to No. 1 in the [Official World Golf Ranking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Official_World_Golf_Ranking "Official World Golf Ranking").[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-No.1-78) After a lackluster 1998, Woods finished the 1999 season with eight wins, including the [PGA Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_PGA_Championship "1999 PGA Championship"), a feat not achieved since [Johnny Miller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johnny_Miller "Johnny Miller") did it in 1974.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-Truth-79)[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-PGAPOY-80)

Woods was severely myopic; his eyesight had a rating of 11 [diopters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dioptre "Dioptre"). In order to correct this problem, he underwent successful [laser eye surgery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Refractive_surgery "Refractive surgery") in 1999,[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-81) and he immediately resumed winning tour events. In 2007, his vision again began to deteriorate, and he underwent laser eye surgery a second time.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-82) In 2000, Woods won six consecutive events on the PGA Tour, the longest winning streak since [Ben Hogan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Hogan "Ben Hogan") accomplished the feat in 1948. One of these victories was the [U.S. Open](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_U.S._Open_(golf) "2000 U.S. Open (golf)"), where he broke or tied nine tournament records in what _Sports Illustrated_ called "the greatest performance in golf history," winning by a record 15-stroke margin and earning $800,000.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-83) With the victory, Woods became the only golfer in history to have won the U.S. Junior Amateur, U.S. Amateur, and U.S. Open.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-84) At age 24, he became the youngest golfer to achieve the Career [Grand Slam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Slam_(golf) "Grand Slam (golf)").[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-10Years3-85) At the end of 2000, Woods had won nine of the twenty PGA Tour events he entered and had broken the record for lowest scoring average in tour history. He was named the _Sports Illustrated_ Sportsman of the Year, the only athlete to be honored twice, and was ranked by Golf Digest magazine as the twelfth-best golfer of all time.[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-86)

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a3/TigerWoods2004RyderCup1.jpg/250px-TigerWoods2004RyderCup1.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:TigerWoods2004RyderCup1.jpg)

Woods at the [2004 Ryder Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_Ryder_Cup "2004 Ryder Cup")

When Woods won the [2001 Masters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2001_Masters_Tournament "2001 Masters Tournament"), he became the only player to win four consecutive major professional golf titles, although not in the same calendar year. This achievement came to be known as the "Tiger Slam".[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-87) Following a stellar 2001 and 2002 in which he continued to dominate the tour, Woods's career hit a slump.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-Truth-79)[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-Swing-88) He did not win a major in 2003 or 2004. In September 2004, [Vijay Singh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vijay_Singh "Vijay Singh") overtook Woods in the Official World Golf Rankings, ending Woods's record streak of 264 weeks at No. 1.[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-89)

Woods rebounded in 2005, winning six PGA Tour events and reclaiming the top spot in July after swapping it back and forth with Singh over the first half of the year.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-Doral05-90)

Woods began dominantly in 2006, winning his first two PGA tournaments but failing to capture his fifth Masters championship in April.[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-91) Following the death of his father in May, Woods took some time off from the tour and appeared rusty upon his return at the U.S. Open at [Winged Foot Golf Club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winged_Foot_Golf_Club "Winged Foot Golf Club"), where he missed the cut.[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-92) However, he quickly returned to form and ended the year by winning six consecutive tour events. At the season's close, Woods had 54 total wins that included 12 majors; he broke the tour records for both total wins and total majors wins over eleven seasons.[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-Assoc06-93)

Woods continued to excel in 2007 and the first part of 2008. In April 2008, he underwent knee surgery and missed the next two months on the tour.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-94) Woods returned for the [2008 U.S. Open](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008_U.S._Open_(golf) "2008 U.S. Open (golf)"), where he struggled the first day but ultimately claimed a dramatic sudden death victory over [Rocco Mediate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rocco_Mediate "Rocco Mediate") that followed an 18-hole playoff, after which Mediate said, "This guy does things that are just not normal by any stretch of the imagination," and Kenny Perry added, "He beat everybody on one leg."[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-95) Two days later, Woods announced that he would miss the remainder of the season due to additional knee surgery, and that his knee was more severely damaged than previously revealed, prompting even greater praise for his U.S. Open performance. Woods called it "my greatest ever championship."[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-96) In Woods's absence, television ratings for the remainder of the season suffered a huge decline from 2007.[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-97)

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/33/Tiger_Woods_-_AT%26T_National_tournament_2009.jpg/250px-Tiger_Woods_-_AT%26T_National_tournament_2009.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Tiger_Woods_-_AT&T_National_tournament_2009.jpg)

Woods competing at the third annual Earl Woods Memorial Pro-Am (July 1, 2009)

Woods had a much anticipated return to golf in 2009, when he performed well. His comeback included a spectacular performance at the [2009 Presidents Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2009_Presidents_Cup "2009 Presidents Cup"), but he failed to win a major, the first year since 2004 that he did not do so.[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-98) After his marital infidelities came to light and received massive media coverage at the end of 2009 (see further details below), Woods announced in December that he would be taking an indefinite break from competitive golf.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-legend-8) In February 2010, he delivered a televised apology for his behavior, saying "I was wrong and I was foolish."[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-BBC100223-99) During this period, several companies ended their endorsement deals with Woods.[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-connection-100)

Woods returned to competition in April at the [2010 Masters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Masters_Tournament "2010 Masters Tournament"), where he finished tied for fourth place.[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-101) He followed the Masters with poor showings at the Quail Hollow Championship and the Players Championship, where he withdrew in the fourth round, citing injury.[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-102) Shortly afterward, [Hank Haney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hank_Haney "Hank Haney"), Woods's coach since 2003, resigned the position. In August, Woods hired [Sean Foley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Foley_(golf_instructor) "Sean Foley (golf instructor)") as Haney's replacement. The rest of the season went badly for Woods, who failed to win a single event for the first time since turning professional, while nevertheless finishing the season ranked No. 2 in the world.

In 2011, Woods's performance continued to suffer; this took its toll on his ranking. After falling to No. 7 in March, he rebounded to No. 5 with a strong showing at the [2011 Masters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Masters_Tournament "2011 Masters Tournament"), where he tied for fourth place.[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-auto-103)[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-104) Due to leg injuries incurred at the Masters, he missed several summer stops on the PGA Tour. In July, he fired his longtime caddie [Steve Williams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Williams_(caddie) "Steve Williams (caddie)") (who was shocked by the dismissal), and replaced him on an interim basis with friend Bryon Bell until he hired Joe LaCava.[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-105)[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-106) After returning to tournament play in August, Woods continued to falter, and his ranking gradually fell to a low of #58.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-chevron-10) He rose to No. 50 in mid-November after a third-place finish at the [Emirates Australian Open](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emirates_Australian_Open "Emirates Australian Open"), and broke his winless streak with a victory at December's [Chevron World Challenge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chevron_World_Challenge "Chevron World Challenge").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-chevron-10)[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-107)[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-108)

Woods began his 2012 season with two tournaments (the [Abu Dhabi HSBC Golf Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abu_Dhabi_HSBC_Golf_Championship "Abu Dhabi HSBC Golf Championship") and the [AT&T Pebble Beach National Pro-Am](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AT&T_Pebble_Beach_National_Pro-Am "AT&T Pebble Beach National Pro-Am")) where he started off well but struggled on the final rounds. Following the [WGC-Accenture Match Play Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WGC-Accenture_Match_Play_Championship "WGC-Accenture Match Play Championship"), where he was knocked out in the second round by missing a 5-foot putt,[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-109) Woods revised his putting technique and tied for second at [The Honda Classic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Honda_Classic "The Honda Classic"), with the lowest final-round score in his PGA Tour career. After a short time off due to another leg injury, Woods won the [Arnold Palmer Invitational](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arnold_Palmer_Invitational "Arnold Palmer Invitational"), his first win on the PGA Tour since the [BMW Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BMW_Championship_(PGA_Tour) "BMW Championship (PGA Tour)") in September 2009. Following several dismal performances, Woods notched his 73rd PGA Tour win at the [Memorial Tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Memorial_Tournament "Memorial Tournament") in June, tying [Jack Nicklaus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Nicklaus "Jack Nicklaus") in second place for most PGA Tour victories;[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-110) a month later, Woods surpassed Nicklaus with a win at the [AT&T National](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AT&T_National "AT&T National"), to trail only [Sam Snead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam_Snead "Sam Snead"), who accumulated 82 PGA tour wins.[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-111)

The year 2013 brought a return of Woods's dominating play. In January, he won the [Farmers Insurance Open](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Farmers_Insurance_Open "Farmers Insurance Open") by four shots for his 75th PGA Tour win. It was the seventh time he won the event.[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-112) In March, he won the [WGC-Cadillac Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WGC-Cadillac_Championship "WGC-Cadillac Championship"), also for the seventh time, giving him his 17th WGC title and first since 2009.[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-113) Two weeks later, he won the [Arnold Palmer Invitational](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arnold_Palmer_Invitational "Arnold Palmer Invitational"), winning the event for a record-tying 8th time. The win moved him back to the top of the world rankings.[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-114) To commemorate that achievement, Nike was quick to launch an ad with the tagline "winning takes care of everything".[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-115)

During the [2013 Masters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2013_Masters_Tournament "2013 Masters Tournament"), Woods faced disqualification after unwittingly admitting in a post-round interview with [ESPN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ESPN "ESPN") that he took an illegal drop on the par-5 15th hole when his third shot bounced off the pin and into the water. After further [review of television footage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trial_by_television_in_golf_tournaments "Trial by television in golf tournaments"), Woods was assessed a two-stroke penalty for the drop but was not disqualified.[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-116) He finished tied for fourth in the event. Woods won [The Players Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Players_Championship "The Players Championship") in May 2013, his second career win at the event, notching his fourth win of the 2013 season. It was the quickest he got to four wins in any season of his professional career.

Woods had a poor showing at the [2013 U.S. Open](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2013_U.S._Open_(golf) "2013 U.S. Open (golf)") as a result of an elbow injury that he sustained at [The Players Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Players_Championship "The Players Championship"). In finishing at 13-over-par, he recorded his worst score as a professional and finished 12 strokes behind winner [Justin Rose](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Justin_Rose "Justin Rose"). After a prolonged break because of the injury, during which he missed the [Greenbrier Classic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greenbrier_Classic "Greenbrier Classic") and his own [AT&T National](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AT&T_National "AT&T National"), he returned at the [Open Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2013_Open_Championship "2013 Open Championship") at [Muirfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muirfield "Muirfield"). Despite being in contention all week and beginning the final round only two strokes behind [Lee Westwood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lee_Westwood "Lee Westwood"), he struggled with the speed of the greens and could only manage a 3-over-par 74 that left him tied for 6th place, five strokes behind eventual winner [Phil Mickelson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phil_Mickelson "Phil Mickelson"). Two weeks later, Woods returned to form at the [WGC-Bridgestone Invitational](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2013_WGC-Bridgestone_Invitational "2013 WGC-Bridgestone Invitational"), recording his 5th win of the season and 8th win at the event in its 15-year history. His second-round 61 matched his record score on the PGA Tour and could easily have been a 59 were it not for some short missed birdie putts on the closing holes. This gave him a seven-stroke lead that he held onto for the rest of the tournament. But at the PGA Championship at Oak Hill Country Club, Woods was never in contention, making 2013 his fifth full season where he did not win a major; he was in contention in only two of the four majors in 2013.

After a slow start to 2014, Woods sustained an injury during the final round of [The Honda Classic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Honda_Classic "The Honda Classic") and was unable to finish the tournament. He withdrew after the 13th hole, citing back pain.[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-117) He subsequently competed in the [WGC-Cadillac Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WGC-Cadillac_Championship "WGC-Cadillac Championship") but was visibly in pain during much of the last round. He was forced to skip the [Arnold Palmer Invitational](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arnold_Palmer_Invitational "Arnold Palmer Invitational") at the end of March 2014,[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-118) and after undergoing [back surgery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microdiscectomy "Microdiscectomy"), he announced on April 1 that he would miss the [Masters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masters_Tournament "Masters Tournament") for the first time since 1994.[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-119) Woods returned at the [Quicken Loans National](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quicken_Loans_National "Quicken Loans National") in June, however he said that his expectations for the week were low. He struggled with nearly every aspect of his game and missed the cut. He next played at [The Open Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Open_Championship "The Open Championship"), contested at Hoylake, where Woods had won eight years prior. Woods fired a brilliant 69 in the first round to put himself in contention, but shot 77 on Friday and eventually finished 69th. Despite his back pain, he played at the [2014 PGA Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2014_PGA_Championship "2014 PGA Championship") where he failed to make the cut. On August 25, 2014, Woods and his swing coach Sean Foley parted ways. In the four years under Foley, he won eight times but no majors. He had previously won eight majors with Harmon and six with Haney. Woods said there was currently no timetable to find a replacement swing coach.[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-120)

On February 5, 2015, Woods withdrew from the [Farmers Insurance Open](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Farmers_Insurance_Open "Farmers Insurance Open") after another back injury.[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-121) Woods stated on his website that it was unrelated to his previous surgery and he would take a break from golf until his back healed.[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-122) He returned for the [Masters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Masters_Tournament "2015 Masters Tournament"), finishing in a tie for 17th. In the final round, Woods injured his wrist after his club hit a tree root. He later stated that a bone popped out of his wrist, but he adjusted it back into place and finished the round.[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-123) Woods then missed the cut at the 2015 [U.S. Open](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_U.S._Open_(golf) "2015 U.S. Open (golf)") and [Open Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Open_Championship "2015 Open Championship"), the first time Woods missed the cut at consecutive majors, finishing near the bottom of the leaderboard both times.[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-124) He finished tied for 18th at the [Quicken Loans National](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quicken_Loans_National "Quicken Loans National") on August 2.[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-125) In late August 2015, Woods played quite well at the Wyndham Championship finishing the tournament at 13-under, only four strokes behind the winner, and tied for 10th place.[[124]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-126) Woods offered only a brief comment on the speculation that he was still recovering from [back surgery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microdiscectomy "Microdiscectomy"), saying it was "just my hip" but offering no specifics.[[125]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-127)

Woods had back surgery on September 16, 2015. In late March 2016, he announced that he would miss the [Masters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masters_Tournament "Masters Tournament") while he recovered from the surgery;[[126]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-back-128) he had also missed the 2014 Masters due to a back problem.[[127]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-129) "I'm absolutely making progress, and I'm really happy with how far I've come," he explained in a statement. "But I still have no timetable to return to competitive golf."[[128]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-130) However, he did attend the Masters Champions Dinner on April 5, 2016.[[129]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-131) For the first time in his career, he missed all four majors in one year due to problems with his back. In October 2016, he told Charlie Rose on PBS that he still wanted to break Jack Nicklaus's record of 18 major titles.[[130]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-132) Woods underwent back surgery in December 2016 and spent the next 15 months off the Tour. He made his return to competitive golf in the [Hero World Challenge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hero_World_Challenge "Hero World Challenge").[[131]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-133)

Woods's back problems continued to hinder him in 2017. He missed the cut at the [Farmers Insurance Open](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Farmers_Insurance_Open "Farmers Insurance Open") in January and pulled out of a European Tour event in [Dubai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dubai "Dubai") on February 3. On March 31, Woods announced on his website that he would not be playing in the [2017 Masters Tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_Masters_Tournament "2017 Masters Tournament") despite being cleared to play by his doctors. Woods said that although he was happy with his rehabilitation, he did not feel "tournament ready."[[132]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-cut-134)[[133]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-cuts-135) Woods subsequently told friends, "I'm done".[[134]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-136) On April 20, Woods announced that he had undergone his fourth back surgery since 2014 to alleviate back and leg pain. Recovery time required up to six months, meaning that Woods would spend the rest of the year without playing any professional golf.[[135]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-137) Woods returned to competitive golf at the Hero World Challenge in the Bahamas. He shot rounds of 69–68–75–68 and finished tied for 9th place. His world ranking went from 1,199th to 668th, which was the biggest jump in the world rankings in his career.

On March 11, 2018, he finished one-shot back and tied for second at the Valspar Championship in Florida, his first top-five finish on the PGA Tour since 2013.[[136]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-138) He then tied for sixth with a score of five under par at the [2018 Open Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2018_Open_Championship "2018 Open Championship").[[137]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-139) At the last major of the year, the [2018 PGA Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2018_PGA_Championship "2018 PGA Championship"), Woods finished second, two shots behind the winner [Brooks Koepka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brooks_Koepka "Brooks Koepka"). It was his best result in a major since 2009 (second at the [2009 PGA Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2009_PGA_Championship "2009 PGA Championship")) and moved him up to 26th in the world rankings. His final round of 64 was his best-ever final round in a major.[[138]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-140)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-reid-13)

Woods returned to the winner's circle for the 80th time in his PGA Tour career on September 23, 2018, when he won the season-ending [Tour Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tour_Championship "Tour Championship") at East Lake Golf Club for the second time and that tournament for the third time. He shot rounds of 65–68–65–71 to win by two strokes over [Billy Horschel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billy_Horschel "Billy Horschel").[[139]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-141)

On April 14, 2019, Woods won the [Masters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_Masters_Tournament "2019 Masters Tournament"), which was his first major championship win in eleven years and his 15th major overall. He finished 13 under par to win by one stroke over [Dustin Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dustin_Johnson "Dustin Johnson"), [Xander Schauffele](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xander_Schauffele "Xander Schauffele") and [Brooks Koepka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brooks_Koepka "Brooks Koepka").[[140]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-142) At age 43, he became the second oldest golfer ever to win the Masters, after [Jack Nicklaus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Nicklaus "Jack Nicklaus") who was 46 when he triumphed in 1986.[[141]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-Crouse14April-143) In August 2019, Woods announced via social media that he underwent knee surgery to repair minor cartilage damage and that he had an arthroscopic procedure during the Tour Championship. In his statement, Woods also confirmed that he was walking and intended on traveling and playing in Japan in October.[[142]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-144)

Woods played in his first [2020 PGA Tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_PGA_Tour "2020 PGA Tour") event at the [Zozo Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zozo_Championship "Zozo Championship") in October 2019, which was the first-ever PGA Tour event played in [Japan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan "Japan"). Woods, who played a highly publicized [skins game](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skins_game "Skins game") earlier in the week at the same course as the Championship, held at least a share of the lead after every round of the rain-delayed tournament, giving him a three stroke victory over [Hideki Matsuyama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hideki_Matsuyama "Hideki Matsuyama").[[143]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-145) The win was Woods's 82nd on Tour, tying him with [Sam Snead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam_Snead "Sam Snead") for the most victories all time on the PGA Tour.[[144]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-146)[[145]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-147)

In December 2020, Woods had microdiscectomy surgery on his back for the fifth time.[[146]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-148) The operation was to remove a pressurized disc fragment that was pinching his nerve and causing him pain during the PNC Championship. Woods returned to play in his first professional tournament since his 2021 motor vehicle crash at the [2022 Masters Tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Masters_Tournament "2022 Masters Tournament"). He made the cut and finished in 47th place at 13-over par, 23 shots behind the winner [Scottie Scheffler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scottie_Scheffler "Scottie Scheffler").[[147]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-149)

In August 2022, Woods, [Rory McIlroy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rory_McIlroy "Rory McIlroy"), [Mike McCarley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_McCarley "Mike McCarley"), and the PGA Tour announced the formation of [TGL](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TGL_(golf_league) "TGL (golf league)"), a six-team [virtual golfing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virtual_golf "Virtual golf") league.[[148]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-150) In November 2023, Woods revealed himself as an co-owner and player for [Jupiter Links Golf Club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jupiter_Links_Golf_Club "Jupiter Links Golf Club"), founded with investments by [David Blitzer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Blitzer "David Blitzer").[[149]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-151)

### Tiger-proofing

Early in Woods's career, a small number of golf industry analysts expressed concern about his impact on the competitiveness of the game and the public appeal of professional golf. Sportswriter Bill Lyon of [Knight Ridder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Knight_Ridder "Knight Ridder") asked in a column, "Isn't Tiger Woods actually bad for golf?" (though Lyon ultimately concluded that he was not).[[192]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-Bad-194) At first, some pundits feared that Woods would drive the spirit of competition out of the game of golf by making existing courses obsolete and relegating opponents to simply competing for second place each week.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

A related effect was measured by [University of California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_California,_Berkeley "University of California, Berkeley") economist Jennifer Brown, who found that other golfers scored worse when competing against Woods than when he was not in the tournament. The scores of highly skilled golfers are nearly one stroke higher when playing against Woods. This effect was larger when he was on winning streaks and disappeared during his well-publicized slump in 2003–04. Brown explains the results by noting that competitors of similar skill can hope to win by increasing their level of effort, but that, when facing a "superstar" competitor, extra exertion does not significantly raise one's level of winning while increasing risk of injury or exhaustion, leading to reduced effort.[[193]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-195) Many courses in the PGA Tour rotation (including major championship sites like [Augusta National](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augusta_National_Golf_Club "Augusta National Golf Club")) have added yardage to their tees in an effort to reduce the advantage of long hitters like Woods, in a strategy that became known as "Tiger-proofing".[[194]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-196) Woods said he welcomed the change, in that adding yardage to courses did not affect his ability to win.[[195]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-Open2005-197)

## Career achievements

Main article: [List of career achievements by Tiger Woods](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_career_achievements_by_Tiger_Woods "List of career achievements by Tiger Woods")

Woods has won 82 official [PGA Tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PGA_Tour "PGA Tour") events, including 15 [majors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Men's_major_golf_championships "Men's major golf championships"). He is 14–1 when going into the final round of a major with at least a share of the lead. Multiple golf experts have heralded Woods as "the greatest closer in history".[[196]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-198) He has the lowest career scoring average and the largest career earnings of any player in PGA Tour history.

Woods's victory at the [2013 Players Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2013_Players_Championship "2013 Players Championship") also marked a win in his 300th [PGA Tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PGA_Tour "PGA Tour") start.[[197]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-199) He also won golf tournaments in his [100th](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WGC-Bridgestone_Invitational#Winners "WGC-Bridgestone Invitational") (in 2000) and [200th](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Farmers_Insurance_Open#Winners "Farmers Insurance Open") (in 2006) tour starts.[[198]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-200)

Woods has spent the most consecutive and cumulative weeks atop the world rankings. He is one of six players (along with [Gene Sarazen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gene_Sarazen "Gene Sarazen"), [Ben Hogan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Hogan "Ben Hogan"), [Gary Player](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gary_Player "Gary Player"), [Jack Nicklaus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Nicklaus "Jack Nicklaus"), and [Rory McIlroy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rory_McIlroy "Rory McIlroy")) to have won all four major championships in his career, known as the Career Grand Slam, and was the youngest to do so.[[199]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_Woods#cite_note-201) Woods is the only player to have consecutively won all four major championships open to professionals, accomplishing the feat in the 2000–2001 seasons.
