_**Sports Illustrated**_ (_**SI**_) is  an American [sports magazine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_magazine "Sports magazine") first published in August 1954. Founded by [Stuart Scheftel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stuart_Scheftel "Stuart Scheftel"), it was the first magazine with a circulation of over one million to win the [National Magazine Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Magazine_Awards "National Magazine Awards") for General Excellence twice. It is also known for its annual [swimsuit issue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated_Swimsuit_Issue "Sports Illustrated Swimsuit Issue"), which has been published since 1964, and has spawned other complementary media works and products.

Owned until 2018 by [Time Inc.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_Inc. "Time Inc."), it was sold to [Authentic Brands Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Authentic_Brands_Group "Authentic Brands Group") (ABG) following the sale of Time Inc. to [Meredith Corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meredith_Corporation "Meredith Corporation"). The Arena Group (formerly theMaven, Inc.) was subsequently awarded a 10-year license to operate the _Sports Illustrated_–branded editorial operations, while ABG [licenses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brand_licensing "Brand licensing") the brand for other non-editorial ventures and products. In January 2024, The Arena Group missed a quarterly licensing payment, leading ABG to terminate the company's license. Arena, in turn, laid off the publication's editorial staff.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-4)

In March 2024, ABG licensed the publishing rights to [Minute Media](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minute_Media "Minute Media") in a 10-year deal, jointly announcing that the print and digital editions would be revived by rehiring some of the editorial staff.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-:0-5) On May 17, 2024, _Sports Illustrated_ failed to deliver a print copy of the publication for the month to its subscribers for the first time in the magazine's 70-year history, according to the _[New York Post](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New\_York\_Post "New York Post")_'s Josh Kosman.

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sports_Illustrated&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

### Establishment

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sports_Illustrated&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Establishment")]

There were two previous magazines named _Sports Illustrated_ before the current magazine was launched on August 9, 1954.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-mfloss-6) In 1936, [Stuart Scheftel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stuart_Scheftel "Stuart Scheftel") created _Sports Illustrated_ with a target market of sportsmen. He published the magazine monthly from 1936 to 1942. The magazine focused on golf, tennis, and skiing with articles on the major sports. He then sold the name to Dell Publications, which released _Sports Illustrated_ in 1949 and this version lasted six issues before closing. Dell's version focused on major sports (baseball, basketball, boxing) and competed on magazine racks against _Sports_ and other monthly sports magazines. During the 1940s, these magazines were monthly, which prevented them from covering current events. There was no large-base, general, weekly sports magazine with a national following on actual active events. It was then that _[Time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time\_(magazine) "Time (magazine)")_ patriarch [Henry Luce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Luce "Henry Luce") began considering whether his company should attempt to fill that gap. At the time, many believed sports was beneath the attention of serious journalism and did not think sports news could fill a weekly magazine, especially during the winter. A number of advisers to Luce, including _[Life](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Life\_(magazine) "Life (magazine)")_ magazine's Ernest Havemann, tried to kill the idea, but Luce, who was not a sports fan, decided the time was right.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-7)

Luce and editors of the planned magazine met in 1954 at [Pine Lakes Country Club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ocean_Forest_Country_Club "Ocean Forest Country Club"), the oldest golf course in [Myrtle Beach, South Carolina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Myrtle_Beach,_South_Carolina "Myrtle Beach, South Carolina"). The course's pro shop has a plaque mentioning the meetings, and the plaque also states that the first issue was given to the course. It is on display there. Myrtle Beach Area Golf Course Owners Association executive director Tracy Conner credits the magazine with making Myrtle Beach a golf destination.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-8)

Many at [Time-Life](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_Life "Time Life") scoffed at Luce's idea; in his [Pulitzer Prize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pulitzer_Prize "Pulitzer Prize")–winning biography, _Luce and His Empire_, [W. A. Swanberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/W._A._Swanberg "W. A. Swanberg") wrote that the company's intellectuals dubbed the proposed magazine "Muscle", "Jockstrap", and "Sweat Socks". Launched on August 9, 1954, it was not profitable (and would not be for 12 years)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-9) and not particularly well-run at first, but Luce's timing was good. The popularity of spectator sports in the United States was about to explode, and that popularity came to be driven largely by three things: economic prosperity, television, and _Sports Illustrated_.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-10)

The early issues of the magazine seemed caught between two opposing views of its audience. Much of the subject matter was directed at upper-class activities such as [yachting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yachting "Yachting"), [polo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polo "Polo") and [safaris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Safari "Safari"), but upscale would-be [advertisers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Advertising "Advertising") were unconvinced that [sports fans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_fan "Sports fan") were a significant part of their market.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-11)

### Color printing

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sports_Illustrated&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Color printing")]

In 1965, [offset printing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Offset_printing "Offset printing") began. This allowed the color pages of the magazine to be printed overnight, not only producing crisper and brighter images, but also finally enabling the editors to merge the best color with the latest news. By 1967, the magazine was printing 200 pages of "fast color" a year; in 1983, _SI_ became the first American full-color newsweekly. An intense rivalry developed between [photographers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photojournalism "Photojournalism"), particularly [Walter Iooss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Iooss "Walter Iooss") and [Neil Leifer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Leifer "Neil Leifer"), to get a decisive cover shot that would be on newsstands and in mailboxes only a few days later.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-12)

In the late 1970s and early 1980s, during [Gilbert Rogin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gilbert_Rogin "Gilbert Rogin")'s term as Managing Editor, the feature stories of [Frank Deford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Deford "Frank Deford") became the magazine's anchor. "Bonus pieces" on [Pete Rozelle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Rozelle "Pete Rozelle"), [Woody Hayes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woody_Hayes "Woody Hayes"), [Bear Bryant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bear_Bryant "Bear Bryant"), [Howard Cosell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Howard_Cosell "Howard Cosell") and others became some of the most quoted sources about these figures, and Deford established a reputation as one of the best writers of the time.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-13)

### Expansion of sports coverage

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sports_Illustrated&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Expansion of sports coverage")]

After more than a decade of steady losses, the magazine's fortunes finally turned around in the 1960s when [Andre Laguerre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andre_Laguerre "Andre Laguerre") became its managing editor. A European correspondent for Time, Inc., who later became chief of the Time-Life news bureaux in Paris and London (for a time he ran both simultaneously), Laguerre attracted Henry Luce's attention in 1956 with his singular coverage of the [Winter Olympic Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winter_Olympic_Games "Winter Olympic Games") in [Cortina d'Ampezzo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cortina_d'Ampezzo "Cortina d'Ampezzo"), Italy, which became the core of _SI'_ s coverage of those games. In May 1956, Luce brought Laguerre to New York to become the assistant managing editor of the magazine. He was named managing editor in 1960, and he more than doubled the circulation by instituting a system of departmental editors, redesigning the internal format, and inaugurating the unprecedented use in a news magazine of full-color photographic coverage of the week's sports events. He was also one of the first to sense the rise of national interest in professional [football](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_football "American football").[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-14)

Laguerre also instituted the innovative concept of one long story at the end of every issue, which he called the "bonus piece". These well-written, in-depth articles helped to distinguish _Sports Illustrated_ from other sports publications, and helped launch the careers of such legendary writers as [Frank Deford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Deford "Frank Deford"), who in March 2010 wrote of Laguerre, "He smoked cigars and drank Scotch and made the sun move across the heavens ... His genius as an editor was that he made you want to please him, but he wanted you to do that by writing in your own distinct way."[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-15) Laguerre is also credited with the conception and creation of the annual _[Swimsuit Issue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swimsuit\_Issue "Swimsuit Issue")_.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

In 1984, [Mark Mulvoy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Mulvoy "Mark Mulvoy") became the youngest [managing editor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Managing_editor "Managing editor") in the magazine's history.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-Stubbs-2023-16)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-Parquette-2024-17) He sought for _Sports Illustrated_ "to be the conscience of sports" through [investigative journalism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Investigative_journalism "Investigative journalism").[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-Parquette-2024-17) He established the Golf Plus insert for the older golfing audience,[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-18) established _[Sports Illustrated Kids](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports\_Illustrated\_Kids "Sports Illustrated Kids")_ for a younger audience, and doubled the swimsuit issue to 40 pages.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-19) The swimsuit issue became an annual special edition, and profits for _Sports Illustrated_ more than quadrupled.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-Stubbs-2023-16) In 1986, co-owned property [HBO/Cannon Video](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Home_Box_Office,_Inc. "Home Box Office, Inc.") had inked a pact to produce video versions of the magazine for $20 on the sell-through market, running just 30–45 minutes on the tape.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-20) In 1990, Time Inc. merged with [Warner Communications](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warner_Communications "Warner Communications") to form the media conglomerate [Time Warner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_Warner "Time Warner"). _Sports Illustrated_ acquired FanNation.com in 2007 to compete in the [Web 2.0](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Web_2.0 "Web 2.0") market; the site [aggregated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/News_aggregator "News aggregator") sports news and allowed [user-generated content](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/User-generated_content "User-generated content").[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-21) In 2014, Time Inc. was spun off from Time Warner.

### Sale to Authentic Brands Group, Maven

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sports_Illustrated&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Sale to Authentic Brands Group, Maven")]

In 2018, [Meredith Corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meredith_Corporation "Meredith Corporation") acquired parent company [Time Inc.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_Inc. "Time Inc.") Meredith planned to sell _Sports Illustrated_ due to not aligning with its lifestyle properties.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-22)[Authentic Brands Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Authentic_Brands_Group "Authentic Brands Group") announced its intent to acquire _Sports Illustrated_ for $110 million the next year, stating that it would leverage its brand and other assets for new opportunities that "stay close to the DNA and the heritage of the brand." Upon the announcement, Meredith would enter into a licensing agreement to continue as publisher of the _Sports Illustrated_ editorial operations for at least the next two years.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-23)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-24) In June 2019, the rights to publish the _Sports Illustrated_ editorial operations were licensed to the digital media company theMaven, Inc. under a 10-year contract, with [Ross Levinsohn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ross_Levinsohn "Ross Levinsohn") as CEO. The company had backed a bid by [Junior Bridgeman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Junior_Bridgeman "Junior Bridgeman") to acquire _SI_.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-25)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-26) In preparation for the closure of the sale to ABG and Maven,[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-27)_[The Wall Street Journal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Wall\_Street\_Journal "The Wall Street Journal")_ reported that there would be _Sports Illustrated_ employee layoffs,[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-28) which was confirmed after the acquisition had closed.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-29)

In October 2019, editor-in-chief Chris Stone stepped down.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-30) Later that month, _Sports Illustrated_ announced its hiring of veteran college sports writer [Pat Forde](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pat_Forde "Pat Forde").[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-31) In January 2020, it announced an editorial partnership with _[The Hockey News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Hockey\_News "The Hockey News")_, focusing on syndication of NHL-related coverage._[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports\_Illustrated#cite\_note-32)_[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-33) In 2021, it announced a similar partnership with _Morning Read_ for golf coverage, with its website being merged into that of _Sports Illustrated_.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-34) It also partnered with [iHeartMedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IHeartMedia "IHeartMedia") to distribute and co-produce [podcasts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Podcast "Podcast").[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-35)

In September 2021, Maven, now known as The Arena Group, acquired the New Jersey–based sports news website _The Spun_, which would integrate into _Sports Illustrated_.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-36) In 2022, ABG announced several non-editorial ventures involving the _Sports Illustrated_ brand, including an apparel line for [JCPenney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/JCPenney "JCPenney") "inspired by iconic moments in sports" (it was not the brand's first foray into clothing, as it launched a branded swimsuit line in conjunction with its _Swimsuit Issue_ in 2018),[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-37) and [resort hotels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Resort_hotel "Resort hotel") in [Orlando](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orlando,_Florida "Orlando, Florida") and [Punta Cana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punta_Cana "Punta Cana").[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-38) In September 2023, it expanded its resorts name licensing through a new partnership with _[Travel + Leisure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Travel\_+\_Leisure "Travel + Leisure")_.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-39)

On November 27, 2023, _[Futurism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Futurism\_(website) "Futurism (website)")_ published an article alleging that _Sports Illustrated_ was publishing AI-generated articles credited to authors who were also AI-generated; the latter practice apparently extended to their profile photos, which the website alleged were sourced from online marketplaces selling such photos.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-40) After _Futurism_ reached out to The Arena Group, the magazine purportedly removed some of the implicated writers and republished their articles under other AI-generated authors with notes disclaiming its staff's involvement.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-41)[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-AI_-_CNN-42) In response to the report, a spokesperson for _Sports Illustrated_ claimed that the affected articles were product reviews written without the involvement of AI by AdVon Commerce, a third-party company who they claimed used pseudonyms to "protect author privacy" and had already severed ties with; meanwhile, writers and editors at the magazine sharply criticized the alleged practices.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-AI_-_CNN-42)

On January 5, 2024, The Arena Group missed a $3.75 million quarterly licensing payment to Authentic Brands Group.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-43) Two weeks later, on January 19, Authentic Brands Group terminated its licensing agreement. As a result, The Arena Group announced that it would lay off the entire _Sports Illustrated_ staff.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-44) In March 2024, Authentic Brands Group licensed the publishing rights to [Minute Media](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minute_Media "Minute Media") in a 10-year deal, jointly announcing that the print and digital editions would be revived by rehiring some of the editorial staff.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-:0-5) Minute converted the Fan Nation-branded sites to "On SI".[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-45)[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-46) In August 2024, Minute Media and [RTA Media Holdings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Race_Team_Alliance "Race Team Alliance") (and RTA's brand _Racing America_) entered into a partnership, forming _Racing America on SI_. This partnership allows Racing America's coverage of [NASCAR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASCAR "NASCAR") and grassroots racing to be presented to a wider audience through Sports Illustrated's platforms.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-47)

## Regular segments

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sports_Illustrated&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Regular segments")]

*   Who's Hot, Who's Not: a feature on who is on a roll and who is going to fold.
*   Inside the [NFL](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Football_League "National Football League"), [MLB](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Major_League_Baseball "Major League Baseball"), [NHL](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Hockey_League "National Hockey League"), [NBA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Basketball_Association "National Basketball Association"), [College Football](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/College_Football "College Football"), [College Basketball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/College_Basketball "College Basketball"), [NASCAR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASCAR "NASCAR"), [Golf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golf "Golf"), [Boxing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boxing "Boxing"), [Horse Racing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horse_racing "Horse racing"), [Soccer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_football "Association football"), and [Tennis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tennis "Tennis") (sports vary from issue to issue): a section where writers from each sport address the latest news and rumors in their respective fields.
*   Faces in the Crowd: a section which honors talented amateur athletes and their accomplishments.
*   The Point After: a back-page column featuring a rotation of SI writers as well as other contributors. Content varies from stories to opinion, focusing on both the world of sports and the role sports play in society.

### American Sportswear Designer Award (ASDA Awards)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sports_Illustrated&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: American Sportswear Designer Award (ASDA Awards)")]

In 1956, Sports Illustrated began presenting annual awards to fashion designers who had excelled in the field of sportswear/activewear. The first ASDAs of 1956, presented to [Claire McCardell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claire_McCardell "Claire McCardell") with a separate Designer of the Year award to [Rudi Gernreich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudi_Gernreich "Rudi Gernreich"), were chosen following a vote of 200 American top retailers.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-48) The following year, the voting pool had increased to 400 fashion industry experts, including [Dorothy Shaver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dorothy_Shaver "Dorothy Shaver") and [Stanley Marcus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanley_Marcus "Stanley Marcus"), when [Sydney Wragge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sydney_Wragge "Sydney Wragge") and [Bill Atkinson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Atkinson_(designer) "Bill Atkinson (designer)") received the awards.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-49) The Italian designer [Emilio Pucci](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emilio_Pucci "Emilio Pucci") was the first non-American to receive the award in 1961.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-50) The awards were presented up until at least 1963, when [Marc Bohan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Bohan "Marc Bohan") received the prize.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-51) Other winners include [Jeanne S. Campbell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeanne_S._Campbell "Jeanne S. Campbell"), [Bonnie Cashin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bonnie_Cashin "Bonnie Cashin"), and [Rose Marie Reid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rose_Marie_Reid "Rose Marie Reid") who formed the first all-women winning group in 1958.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-52)

### Sportsperson of the Year

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sports_Illustrated&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Sportsperson of the Year")]

Main article: [Sports Illustrated Sportsperson of the Year](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated_Sportsperson_of_the_Year "Sports Illustrated Sportsperson of the Year")

Since 1954, _Sports Illustrated_ has annually presented the [Sportsperson of the Year](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated_Sportsperson_of_the_Year "Sports Illustrated Sportsperson of the Year") award to "the athlete or team whose performance that year most embodies the spirit of sportsmanship and achievement."[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-Sportsmen-54)[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-55)[Roger Bannister](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roger_Bannister "Roger Bannister") won the first-ever Sportsman of the Year award thanks to his record-breaking time of 3:59.4 for a mile, the first-ever time a mile had been run under four minutes.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-Sportsmen-54)[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-56) Both men and women have won the award, originally called "Sportsman of the Year" and renamed "Sportswoman of the Year" or "Sportswomen of the Year" when applicable; it is currently known as "Sportsperson of the Year."

#### Recent winners

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sports_Illustrated&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Recent winners")]

The 2017 award winners were [Houston Texans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston_Texans "Houston Texans") defensive end [J. J. Watt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J._J._Watt "J. J. Watt") and [Houston Astros](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston_Astros "Houston Astros") second baseman [Jose Altuve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jose_Altuve "Jose Altuve").[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-57) Both athletes were recognized for their efforts in helping rebuild the city of Houston following [Hurricane Harvey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Harvey "Hurricane Harvey") in addition to Altuve being a part of the Astros team that won the franchise's first [World Series in 2017](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_World_Series "2017 World Series").[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-58) The 2018 winners were the [Golden State Warriors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_State_Warriors "Golden State Warriors") as a team for winning their third NBA Title in four years.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-59) The 2021 winner was [Tom Brady](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Brady "Tom Brady") for his [Super Bowl LV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_LV "Super Bowl LV") win.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-60) The 2023 winner was [Deion Sanders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deion_Sanders "Deion Sanders"), coach of the [Colorado Buffaloes football](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colorado_Buffaloes_football "Colorado Buffaloes football") team.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-61)

### _Sports Illustrated'_ s Muhammad Ali Legacy Award

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sports_Illustrated&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Sports Illustrated's Muhammad Ali Legacy Award")]

In 2015, the magazine renamed its Sportsman Legacy Award to the _Sports Illustrated'_ s [Muhammad Ali](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_Ali "Muhammad Ali") Legacy Award. The annual award was originally created in 2008 and honors former "sports figures who embody the ideals of sportsmanship, leadership and philanthropy as vehicles for changing the world." Ali first appeared on the magazine's cover in 1963 and went on to be featured on numerous covers during his storied career. His widow, Lonnie Ali, is consulted when choosing a recipient.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-63) In 2017, football quarterback [Colin Kaepernick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colin_Kaepernick "Colin Kaepernick") was honored with the Award, which was presented by [Beyoncé](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beyonc%C3%A9 "Beyoncé").[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-64) In 2018, [WWE](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WWE "WWE") professional wrestler [John Cena](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Cena "John Cena") was honored with the award.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-65)

## Cover history

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sports_Illustrated&action=edit&section=20 "Edit section: Cover history")]

The magazine's cover is the basis of a [sports myth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports-related_curses "Sports-related curses"), known as the [Sports Illustrated cover jinx](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated_cover_jinx "Sports Illustrated cover jinx"). Several athletes and other figures appeared many times on the magazine's cover.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-77)

[Althea Gibson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Althea_Gibson "Althea Gibson") became the first woman on the cover on the September 2, 1957, issue.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-78)

## Spinoffs

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sports_Illustrated&action=edit&section=30 "Edit section: Spinoffs")]

_Sports Illustrated_ has helped to launch a number of related publishing ventures.

*   _[Sports Illustrated Kids](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports\_Illustrated\_Kids "Sports Illustrated Kids")_ magazine (circulation 950,000)[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]
    *   Launched in January 1989
    *   Won the "Distinguished Achievement for Excellence in Educational Publishing" award 11 times
    *   Won the "Parents' Choice Magazine Award" 7 times

*   _Sports Illustrated Almanac_ annuals 
    *   Introduced in 1991
    *   Yearly compilation of sports news and statistics in book form

*   SI.com sports news web site
*   _Sports Illustrated Australia_
    *   Launched in 1992 and lasted 6 issues **

*   _Sports Illustrated Canada_
    *   Was created and published in Canada with US content from 1993 to 1995. Most of the issues appear to have the same cover except they say 'Canadian Edition'. These issues are numbered differently in the listing. A group of the Canadian issues have unique Canadian athletes (hockey mostly) and all the Canadian issues may have some different article content. The advertising may also be Canada-centric.

*   _Sports Illustrated Presents_
    *   Launched in 1989
    *   This is their tribute and special edition issues that are sold both nationally or regionally as stand alone products. **Originally started with Super Bowl Tributes the product became a mainstay in 1993 with Alabama as the NCAA National Football Champions. Today multiple issues are released including regional releases of the NCAA, NBA, NFL, MLB champions along with special events or special people. Advertising deals are also done with Sports Illustrated Presents (Kelloggs).

*   CNNSI.com a 24-hour sports news web site 
    *   Launched on July 17, 1997
    *   Online version of the magazine
    *   The domain name was sold in May 2015[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-84)

*   _[Sports Illustrated Women](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports\_Illustrated\_Women "Sports Illustrated Women")_ magazine (highest circulation 400,000) 
    *   Launched in March 2000
    *   Ceased publication in December 2002 because of a weak advertising climate

*   _Sports Illustrated on Campus_ magazine 
    *   Launched on September 4, 2003
    *   Dedicated to college athletics and the sports interests of college students.
    *   Distributed free on 72 college campuses through a network of college newspapers.
    *   Circulation of one million readers between the ages of 18 and 24.
    *   Ceased publication in December 2005 because of a weak advertising climate

*   Sports Illustrated Online Casino 
    *   Launched on February 7, 2023, in Michigan[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-85)

_**Sports Illustrated**_ (_**SI**_) is  an American [sports magazine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_magazine "Sports magazine") first published in August 1954. Founded by [Stuart Scheftel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stuart_Scheftel "Stuart Scheftel"), it was the first magazine with a circulation of over one million to win the [National Magazine Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Magazine_Awards "National Magazine Awards") for General Excellence twice. It is also known for its annual [swimsuit issue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated_Swimsuit_Issue "Sports Illustrated Swimsuit Issue"), which has been published since 1964, and has spawned other complementary media works and products.

Owned until 2018 by [Time Inc.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_Inc. "Time Inc."), it was sold to [Authentic Brands Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Authentic_Brands_Group "Authentic Brands Group") (ABG) following the sale of Time Inc. to [Meredith Corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meredith_Corporation "Meredith Corporation"). The Arena Group (formerly theMaven, Inc.) was subsequently awarded a 10-year license to operate the _Sports Illustrated_–branded editorial operations, while ABG [licenses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brand_licensing "Brand licensing") the brand for other non-editorial ventures and products. In January 2024, The Arena Group missed a quarterly licensing payment, leading ABG to terminate the company's license. Arena, in turn, laid off the publication's editorial staff.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-4)

In March 2024, ABG licensed the publishing rights to [Minute Media](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minute_Media "Minute Media") in a 10-year deal, jointly announcing that the print and digital editions would be revived by rehiring some of the editorial staff.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-:0-5) On May 17, 2024, _Sports Illustrated_ failed to deliver a print copy of the publication for the month to its subscribers for the first time in the magazine's 70-year history, according to the _[New York Post](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New\_York\_Post "New York Post")_'s Josh Kosman.

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sports_Illustrated&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

### Establishment

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sports_Illustrated&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Establishment")]

There were two previous magazines named _Sports Illustrated_ before the current magazine was launched on August 9, 1954.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-mfloss-6) In 1936, [Stuart Scheftel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stuart_Scheftel "Stuart Scheftel") created _Sports Illustrated_ with a target market of sportsmen. He published the magazine monthly from 1936 to 1942. The magazine focused on golf, tennis, and skiing with articles on the major sports. He then sold the name to Dell Publications, which released _Sports Illustrated_ in 1949 and this version lasted six issues before closing. Dell's version focused on major sports (baseball, basketball, boxing) and competed on magazine racks against _Sports_ and other monthly sports magazines. During the 1940s, these magazines were monthly, which prevented them from covering current events. There was no large-base, general, weekly sports magazine with a national following on actual active events. It was then that _[Time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time\_(magazine) "Time (magazine)")_ patriarch [Henry Luce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Luce "Henry Luce") began considering whether his company should attempt to fill that gap. At the time, many believed sports was beneath the attention of serious journalism and did not think sports news could fill a weekly magazine, especially during the winter. A number of advisers to Luce, including _[Life](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Life\_(magazine) "Life (magazine)")_ magazine's Ernest Havemann, tried to kill the idea, but Luce, who was not a sports fan, decided the time was right.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-7)

Luce and editors of the planned magazine met in 1954 at [Pine Lakes Country Club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ocean_Forest_Country_Club "Ocean Forest Country Club"), the oldest golf course in [Myrtle Beach, South Carolina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Myrtle_Beach,_South_Carolina "Myrtle Beach, South Carolina"). The course's pro shop has a plaque mentioning the meetings, and the plaque also states that the first issue was given to the course. It is on display there. Myrtle Beach Area Golf Course Owners Association executive director Tracy Conner credits the magazine with making Myrtle Beach a golf destination.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-8)

Many at [Time-Life](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_Life "Time Life") scoffed at Luce's idea; in his [Pulitzer Prize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pulitzer_Prize "Pulitzer Prize")–winning biography, _Luce and His Empire_, [W. A. Swanberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/W._A._Swanberg "W. A. Swanberg") wrote that the company's intellectuals dubbed the proposed magazine "Muscle", "Jockstrap", and "Sweat Socks". Launched on August 9, 1954, it was not profitable (and would not be for 12 years)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-9) and not particularly well-run at first, but Luce's timing was good. The popularity of spectator sports in the United States was about to explode, and that popularity came to be driven largely by three things: economic prosperity, television, and _Sports Illustrated_.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-10)

The early issues of the magazine seemed caught between two opposing views of its audience. Much of the subject matter was directed at upper-class activities such as [yachting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yachting "Yachting"), [polo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polo "Polo") and [safaris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Safari "Safari"), but upscale would-be [advertisers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Advertising "Advertising") were unconvinced that [sports fans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_fan "Sports fan") were a significant part of their market.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-11)

### Color printing

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sports_Illustrated&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Color printing")]

In 1965, [offset printing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Offset_printing "Offset printing") began. This allowed the color pages of the magazine to be printed overnight, not only producing crisper and brighter images, but also finally enabling the editors to merge the best color with the latest news. By 1967, the magazine was printing 200 pages of "fast color" a year; in 1983, _SI_ became the first American full-color newsweekly. An intense rivalry developed between [photographers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photojournalism "Photojournalism"), particularly [Walter Iooss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Iooss "Walter Iooss") and [Neil Leifer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Leifer "Neil Leifer"), to get a decisive cover shot that would be on newsstands and in mailboxes only a few days later.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-12)

In the late 1970s and early 1980s, during [Gilbert Rogin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gilbert_Rogin "Gilbert Rogin")'s term as Managing Editor, the feature stories of [Frank Deford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Deford "Frank Deford") became the magazine's anchor. "Bonus pieces" on [Pete Rozelle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Rozelle "Pete Rozelle"), [Woody Hayes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woody_Hayes "Woody Hayes"), [Bear Bryant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bear_Bryant "Bear Bryant"), [Howard Cosell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Howard_Cosell "Howard Cosell") and others became some of the most quoted sources about these figures, and Deford established a reputation as one of the best writers of the time.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-13)

### Expansion of sports coverage

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sports_Illustrated&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Expansion of sports coverage")]

After more than a decade of steady losses, the magazine's fortunes finally turned around in the 1960s when [Andre Laguerre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andre_Laguerre "Andre Laguerre") became its managing editor. A European correspondent for Time, Inc., who later became chief of the Time-Life news bureaux in Paris and London (for a time he ran both simultaneously), Laguerre attracted Henry Luce's attention in 1956 with his singular coverage of the [Winter Olympic Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winter_Olympic_Games "Winter Olympic Games") in [Cortina d'Ampezzo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cortina_d'Ampezzo "Cortina d'Ampezzo"), Italy, which became the core of _SI'_ s coverage of those games. In May 1956, Luce brought Laguerre to New York to become the assistant managing editor of the magazine. He was named managing editor in 1960, and he more than doubled the circulation by instituting a system of departmental editors, redesigning the internal format, and inaugurating the unprecedented use in a news magazine of full-color photographic coverage of the week's sports events. He was also one of the first to sense the rise of national interest in professional [football](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_football "American football").[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-14)

Laguerre also instituted the innovative concept of one long story at the end of every issue, which he called the "bonus piece". These well-written, in-depth articles helped to distinguish _Sports Illustrated_ from other sports publications, and helped launch the careers of such legendary writers as [Frank Deford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Deford "Frank Deford"), who in March 2010 wrote of Laguerre, "He smoked cigars and drank Scotch and made the sun move across the heavens ... His genius as an editor was that he made you want to please him, but he wanted you to do that by writing in your own distinct way."[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-15) Laguerre is also credited with the conception and creation of the annual _[Swimsuit Issue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swimsuit\_Issue "Swimsuit Issue")_.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

In 1984, [Mark Mulvoy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Mulvoy "Mark Mulvoy") became the youngest [managing editor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Managing_editor "Managing editor") in the magazine's history.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-Stubbs-2023-16)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-Parquette-2024-17) He sought for _Sports Illustrated_ "to be the conscience of sports" through [investigative journalism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Investigative_journalism "Investigative journalism").[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-Parquette-2024-17) He established the Golf Plus insert for the older golfing audience,[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-18) established _[Sports Illustrated Kids](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports\_Illustrated\_Kids "Sports Illustrated Kids")_ for a younger audience, and doubled the swimsuit issue to 40 pages.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-19) The swimsuit issue became an annual special edition, and profits for _Sports Illustrated_ more than quadrupled.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-Stubbs-2023-16) In 1986, co-owned property [HBO/Cannon Video](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Home_Box_Office,_Inc. "Home Box Office, Inc.") had inked a pact to produce video versions of the magazine for $20 on the sell-through market, running just 30–45 minutes on the tape.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-20) In 1990, Time Inc. merged with [Warner Communications](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warner_Communications "Warner Communications") to form the media conglomerate [Time Warner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_Warner "Time Warner"). _Sports Illustrated_ acquired FanNation.com in 2007 to compete in the [Web 2.0](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Web_2.0 "Web 2.0") market; the site [aggregated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/News_aggregator "News aggregator") sports news and allowed [user-generated content](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/User-generated_content "User-generated content").[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-21) In 2014, Time Inc. was spun off from Time Warner.

### Sale to Authentic Brands Group, Maven

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sports_Illustrated&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Sale to Authentic Brands Group, Maven")]

In 2018, [Meredith Corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meredith_Corporation "Meredith Corporation") acquired parent company [Time Inc.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_Inc. "Time Inc.") Meredith planned to sell _Sports Illustrated_ due to not aligning with its lifestyle properties.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-22)[Authentic Brands Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Authentic_Brands_Group "Authentic Brands Group") announced its intent to acquire _Sports Illustrated_ for $110 million the next year, stating that it would leverage its brand and other assets for new opportunities that "stay close to the DNA and the heritage of the brand." Upon the announcement, Meredith would enter into a licensing agreement to continue as publisher of the _Sports Illustrated_ editorial operations for at least the next two years.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-23)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-24) In June 2019, the rights to publish the _Sports Illustrated_ editorial operations were licensed to the digital media company theMaven, Inc. under a 10-year contract, with [Ross Levinsohn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ross_Levinsohn "Ross Levinsohn") as CEO. The company had backed a bid by [Junior Bridgeman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Junior_Bridgeman "Junior Bridgeman") to acquire _SI_.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-25)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-26) In preparation for the closure of the sale to ABG and Maven,[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-27)_[The Wall Street Journal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Wall\_Street\_Journal "The Wall Street Journal")_ reported that there would be _Sports Illustrated_ employee layoffs,[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-28) which was confirmed after the acquisition had closed.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-29)

In October 2019, editor-in-chief Chris Stone stepped down.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-30) Later that month, _Sports Illustrated_ announced its hiring of veteran college sports writer [Pat Forde](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pat_Forde "Pat Forde").[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-31) In January 2020, it announced an editorial partnership with _[The Hockey News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Hockey\_News "The Hockey News")_, focusing on syndication of NHL-related coverage._[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports\_Illustrated#cite\_note-32)_[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-33) In 2021, it announced a similar partnership with _Morning Read_ for golf coverage, with its website being merged into that of _Sports Illustrated_.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-34) It also partnered with [iHeartMedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IHeartMedia "IHeartMedia") to distribute and co-produce [podcasts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Podcast "Podcast").[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-35)

In September 2021, Maven, now known as The Arena Group, acquired the New Jersey–based sports news website _The Spun_, which would integrate into _Sports Illustrated_.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-36) In 2022, ABG announced several non-editorial ventures involving the _Sports Illustrated_ brand, including an apparel line for [JCPenney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/JCPenney "JCPenney") "inspired by iconic moments in sports" (it was not the brand's first foray into clothing, as it launched a branded swimsuit line in conjunction with its _Swimsuit Issue_ in 2018),[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-37) and [resort hotels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Resort_hotel "Resort hotel") in [Orlando](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orlando,_Florida "Orlando, Florida") and [Punta Cana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punta_Cana "Punta Cana").[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-38) In September 2023, it expanded its resorts name licensing through a new partnership with _[Travel + Leisure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Travel\_+\_Leisure "Travel + Leisure")_.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-39)

On November 27, 2023, _[Futurism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Futurism\_(website) "Futurism (website)")_ published an article alleging that _Sports Illustrated_ was publishing AI-generated articles credited to authors who were also AI-generated; the latter practice apparently extended to their profile photos, which the website alleged were sourced from online marketplaces selling such photos.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-40) After _Futurism_ reached out to The Arena Group, the magazine purportedly removed some of the implicated writers and republished their articles under other AI-generated authors with notes disclaiming its staff's involvement.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-41)[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-AI_-_CNN-42) In response to the report, a spokesperson for _Sports Illustrated_ claimed that the affected articles were product reviews written without the involvement of AI by AdVon Commerce, a third-party company who they claimed used pseudonyms to "protect author privacy" and had already severed ties with; meanwhile, writers and editors at the magazine sharply criticized the alleged practices.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-AI_-_CNN-42)

On January 5, 2024, The Arena Group missed a $3.75 million quarterly licensing payment to Authentic Brands Group.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-43) Two weeks later, on January 19, Authentic Brands Group terminated its licensing agreement. As a result, The Arena Group announced that it would lay off the entire _Sports Illustrated_ staff.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-44) In March 2024, Authentic Brands Group licensed the publishing rights to [Minute Media](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minute_Media "Minute Media") in a 10-year deal, jointly announcing that the print and digital editions would be revived by rehiring some of the editorial staff.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-:0-5) Minute converted the Fan Nation-branded sites to "On SI".[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-45)[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-46) In August 2024, Minute Media and [RTA Media Holdings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Race_Team_Alliance "Race Team Alliance") (and RTA's brand _Racing America_) entered into a partnership, forming _Racing America on SI_. This partnership allows Racing America's coverage of [NASCAR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASCAR "NASCAR") and grassroots racing to be presented to a wider audience through Sports Illustrated's platforms.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-47)

## Regular segments

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sports_Illustrated&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Regular segments")]

*   Who's Hot, Who's Not: a feature on who is on a roll and who is going to fold.
*   Inside the [NFL](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Football_League "National Football League"), [MLB](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Major_League_Baseball "Major League Baseball"), [NHL](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Hockey_League "National Hockey League"), [NBA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Basketball_Association "National Basketball Association"), [College Football](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/College_Football "College Football"), [College Basketball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/College_Basketball "College Basketball"), [NASCAR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASCAR "NASCAR"), [Golf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golf "Golf"), [Boxing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boxing "Boxing"), [Horse Racing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horse_racing "Horse racing"), [Soccer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_football "Association football"), and [Tennis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tennis "Tennis") (sports vary from issue to issue): a section where writers from each sport address the latest news and rumors in their respective fields.
*   Faces in the Crowd: a section which honors talented amateur athletes and their accomplishments.
*   The Point After: a back-page column featuring a rotation of SI writers as well as other contributors. Content varies from stories to opinion, focusing on both the world of sports and the role sports play in society.

### American Sportswear Designer Award (ASDA Awards)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sports_Illustrated&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: American Sportswear Designer Award (ASDA Awards)")]

In 1956, Sports Illustrated began presenting annual awards to fashion designers who had excelled in the field of sportswear/activewear. The first ASDAs of 1956, presented to [Claire McCardell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claire_McCardell "Claire McCardell") with a separate Designer of the Year award to [Rudi Gernreich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudi_Gernreich "Rudi Gernreich"), were chosen following a vote of 200 American top retailers.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-48) The following year, the voting pool had increased to 400 fashion industry experts, including [Dorothy Shaver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dorothy_Shaver "Dorothy Shaver") and [Stanley Marcus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanley_Marcus "Stanley Marcus"), when [Sydney Wragge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sydney_Wragge "Sydney Wragge") and [Bill Atkinson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Atkinson_(designer) "Bill Atkinson (designer)") received the awards.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-49) The Italian designer [Emilio Pucci](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emilio_Pucci "Emilio Pucci") was the first non-American to receive the award in 1961.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-50) The awards were presented up until at least 1963, when [Marc Bohan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Bohan "Marc Bohan") received the prize.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-51) Other winners include [Jeanne S. Campbell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeanne_S._Campbell "Jeanne S. Campbell"), [Bonnie Cashin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bonnie_Cashin "Bonnie Cashin"), and [Rose Marie Reid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rose_Marie_Reid "Rose Marie Reid") who formed the first all-women winning group in 1958.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-52)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sports_Illustrated&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Sportsperson of the Year")]

Main article: [Sports Illustrated Sportsperson of the Year](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated_Sportsperson_of_the_Year "Sports Illustrated Sportsperson of the Year")

Since 1954, _Sports Illustrated_ has annually presented the [Sportsperson of the Year](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated_Sportsperson_of_the_Year "Sports Illustrated Sportsperson of the Year") award to "the athlete or team whose performance that year most embodies the spirit of sportsmanship and achievement."[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-Sportsmen-54)[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-55)[Roger Bannister](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roger_Bannister "Roger Bannister") won the first-ever Sportsman of the Year award thanks to his record-breaking time of 3:59.4 for a mile, the first-ever time a mile had been run under four minutes.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-Sportsmen-54)[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-56) Both men and women have won the award, originally called "Sportsman of the Year" and renamed "Sportswoman of the Year" or "Sportswomen of the Year" when applicable; it is currently known as "Sportsperson of the Year."

#### Recent winners

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sports_Illustrated&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Recent winners")]

The 2017 award winners were [Houston Texans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston_Texans "Houston Texans") defensive end [J. J. Watt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J._J._Watt "J. J. Watt") and [Houston Astros](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston_Astros "Houston Astros") second baseman [Jose Altuve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jose_Altuve "Jose Altuve").[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-57) Both athletes were recognized for their efforts in helping rebuild the city of Houston following [Hurricane Harvey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Harvey "Hurricane Harvey") in addition to Altuve being a part of the Astros team that won the franchise's first [World Series in 2017](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_World_Series "2017 World Series").[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-58) The 2018 winners were the [Golden State Warriors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_State_Warriors "Golden State Warriors") as a team for winning their third NBA Title in four years.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-59) The 2021 winner was [Tom Brady](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Brady "Tom Brady") for his [Super Bowl LV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_LV "Super Bowl LV") win.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-60) The 2023 winner was [Deion Sanders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deion_Sanders "Deion Sanders"), coach of the [Colorado Buffaloes football](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colorado_Buffaloes_football "Colorado Buffaloes football") team.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-61)

### _Sports Illustrated'_ s Muhammad Ali Legacy Award

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sports_Illustrated&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Sports Illustrated's Muhammad Ali Legacy Award")]

In 2015, the magazine renamed its Sportsman Legacy Award to the _Sports Illustrated'_ s [Muhammad Ali](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_Ali "Muhammad Ali") Legacy Award. The annual award was originally created in 2008 and honors former "sports figures who embody the ideals of sportsmanship, leadership and philanthropy as vehicles for changing the world." Ali first appeared on the magazine's cover in 1963 and went on to be featured on numerous covers during his storied career. His widow, Lonnie Ali, is consulted when choosing a recipient.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-63) In 2017, football quarterback [Colin Kaepernick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colin_Kaepernick "Colin Kaepernick") was honored with the Award, which was presented by [Beyoncé](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beyonc%C3%A9 "Beyoncé").[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-64) In 2018, [WWE](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WWE "WWE") professional wrestler [John Cena](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Cena "John Cena") was honored with the award.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-65)

## Cover history

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sports_Illustrated&action=edit&section=20 "Edit section: Cover history")]

The magazine's cover is the basis of a [sports myth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports-related_curses "Sports-related curses"), known as the [Sports Illustrated cover jinx](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated_cover_jinx "Sports Illustrated cover jinx"). Several athletes and other figures appeared many times on the magazine's cover.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-77)

[Althea Gibson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Althea_Gibson "Althea Gibson") became the first woman on the cover on the September 2, 1957, issue.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-78)

## Spinoffs

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sports_Illustrated&action=edit&section=30 "Edit section: Spinoffs")]

_Sports Illustrated_ has helped to launch a number of related publishing ventures.

*   _[Sports Illustrated Kids](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports\_Illustrated\_Kids "Sports Illustrated Kids")_ magazine (circulation 950,000)[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]
    *   Launched in January 1989
    *   Won the "Distinguished Achievement for Excellence in Educational Publishing" award 11 times
    *   Won the "Parents' Choice Magazine Award" 7 times

*   _Sports Illustrated Almanac_ annuals 
    *   Introduced in 1991
    *   Yearly compilation of sports news and statistics in book form

*   SI.com sports news web site
*   _Sports Illustrated Australia_
    *   Launched in 1992 and lasted 6 issues **

*   _Sports Illustrated Canada_
    *   Was created and published in Canada with US content from 1993 to 1995. Most of the issues appear to have the same cover except they say 'Canadian Edition'. These issues are numbered differently in the listing. A group of the Canadian issues have unique Canadian athletes (hockey mostly) and all the Canadian issues may have some different article content. The advertising may also be Canada-centric.

*   _Sports Illustrated Presents_
    *   Launched in 1989
    *   This is their tribute and special edition issues that are sold both nationally or regionally as stand alone products. **Originally started with Super Bowl Tributes the product became a mainstay in 1993 with Alabama as the NCAA National Football Champions. Today multiple issues are released including regional releases of the NCAA, NBA, NFL, MLB champions along with special events or special people. Advertising deals are also done with Sports Illustrated Presents (Kelloggs).

*   CNNSI.com a 24-hour sports news web site 
    *   Launched on July 17, 1997
    *   Online version of the magazine
    *   The domain name was sold in May 2015[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-84)

*   _[Sports Illustrated Women](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports\_Illustrated\_Women "Sports Illustrated Women")_ magazine (highest circulation 400,000) 
    *   Launched in March 2000
    *   Ceased publication in December 2002 because of a weak advertising climate

*   _Sports Illustrated on Campus_ magazine 
    *   Launched on September 4, 2003
    *   Dedicated to college athletics and the sports interests of college students.
    *   Distributed free on 72 college campuses through a network of college newspapers.
    *   Circulation of one million readers between the ages of 18 and 24.
    *   Ceased publication in December 2005 because of a weak advertising climate

*   Sports Illustrated Online Casino 
    *   Launched on February 7, 2023, in Michigan[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-85)
    *   Operated in co-operation with [888 Holdings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/888_Holdings "888 Holdings")[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-86)
    *   Also includes Sports Illustrated Sportsbook which launched in September 2021[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-87)

*   _Esports Illustrated_
    *   Launched in March 2023 in partnership with Gaud-Hammer Gaming Group.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated#cite_note-88)
